Cyclic Voltammetry · Poster Companion

The Manufactured Capacitance

The ν/ν½ decomposition is the field's default way to split cyclic-voltammetry current into “capacitive” and “faradaic” parts. From Butler–Volmer kinetics and semi-infinite diffusion, we show it invents capacitance that isn't there — reporting a near-perfect R² while it does — and that a single local Damköhler number predicts exactly where it fails.

01 The problem

Battery or capacitor? The answer hides in one current

Deconvoluting faradaic (redox) from non-faradaic (capacitive) current is a central challenge in electrochemical energy storage. The two overlap across the same potential window and cannot be told apart by inspection — yet their ratio decides whether a material behaves as a battery or a capacitor, and sets the trade-off between energy and power density.

Cyclic voltammetry is the conventional tool: fast, and it probes the electrode across timescales by varying the scan rate ν. But the very information density that makes CV powerful — thermodynamics, kinetics, and transport folded into one i–E curve — is what makes separating the currents so hard. The theoretical frameworks for doing it remain underdeveloped, so the field fell back on empirical scaling.

02 The standard method

The ν/ν½ decomposition

The dominant approach writes the current at each potential as a sum of two power laws in scan rate and fits the coefficients by ordinary least squares, separately at every potential, across a set of scan rates:

i(E) = k₁·ν + k₂·ν1/2k₁ — capacitive coefficient (double-layer charging, ∝ ν)  ·  k₂ — faradaic coefficient (diffusion, ∝ ν½)

The faradaic ν½ term traces to Randles–Ševčík: for a fully reversible reaction with semi-infinite diffusion, the peak current scales as ν½. The capacitive ν term reflects the observation that double-layer charging scales linearly with ν. Lindström (1997) formalized the power-law ansatz i ∝ νb, with the exponent read as a diagnostic: b = 0.5 for diffusion control, b = 1 for surface confinement. Dunn (2007) turned it into the pointwise decomposition now applied routinely to oxides, MXenes, phosphates, and intercalation compounds.

The catch: Randles–Ševčík's ν½ holds only at the peak, and only in the reversible limit. Extending it across the whole potential window and the entire reversibility continuum was an extrapolation adopted without first-principles justification — and the formula assumes k₁ is constant, while in practice it drifts with potential. An internal inconsistency on the method's own terms.

“A high R² tells you the sum was reproduced. It tells you nothing about whether the split was right.”

The central result

03 Why it breaks

Two failures: one physical, one statistical

Benchmarked against an exact Butler–Volmer + diffusion simulation, the method returns physically faithful coefficients only in a narrow, reversible corner — while reporting R² ≈ 1 everywhere. Two distinct issues underlie the breakdown.

1 — The physics: b is not 0.5

The true scan-rate exponent is a continuous, potential-dependent function b(E). It approaches the ideal diffusive value 0.5 only in the highly reversible limit; as reversibility decreases, b falls continuously below 0.5. A single fixed exponent cannot represent a continuously varying kinetic response, so the assumed ν½ over-predicts the faradaic term wherever kinetics are sluggish.

2 — The statistics: least squares hides it

OLS minimizes the absolute residual, so it fits the largest signal — the faradaic current — most accurately. The small faradaic scaling mismatch is then absorbed into the k₁·ν capacitive term. When the faradaic current is an order of magnitude larger than the capacitive one, that mismatch is amplified on the way in: a tiny faradaic error becomes a large spurious capacitance. Worse, the two basis functions {ν, ν½} are strongly collinear over a typical scan-rate window, so the split between k₁ and k₂ is poorly determined even when their sum reproduces the data.

  • The two-term basis is exact in the reversible column (ε̃k₁ → 0).
  • Toward the sluggish limit it assigns a large spurious capacitive current (|ε̃k₁| → 1 through the peak) — while R² stays ≈ 1.
  • The error is largest exactly where the true capacitance is small and kinetics are slow — the regime where a capacitive assignment is least justified and most often invoked.

04 The scaling theory

One number governs every point: the local Damköhler number

The structure of b(E) is not arbitrary. Starting from the exact Volterra equation of sweep voltammetry and freezing the memory integral over the elapsed time t̃ = (ηi−η)/σ, the theory produces a single local Damköhler number Da(η) — the ratio of Butler–Volmer reaction velocity to the diffusive supply velocity of the locally grown layer — that controls every point of the voltammogram:

Da(η) = Λ · (ηi−η)1/2 · [ e−αη + κD−1/2 e(1−α)η ]η = F(E−E°)/RT  ·  Λ = k°/√(DOσ), σ = Fν/RT  ·  κD = DR/DO  ·  Λ is the Matsuda–Ayabe / Nicholson global number

Because at fixed η the numerator of the current is scan-rate–independent while Da ∝ ν−1/2, the local exponent follows a one-variable master curve — it depends on Da alone:

b(η) = ½ − 1⁄2(1 + Da(η))b → ½ as Da → ∞ (reversible, diffusion-limited)  ·  b → 0 as Da → 0 (sluggish, kinetically frozen)

Overlay contours of constant Da on the measured b(E, Λ) map and the color bands run parallel to the iso-Da contours, not to either axis: the pointwise exponent collapses onto the local Damköhler number, not the single wave-level ψ. That is the organizing claim — and the next panel lets you walk the whole map yourself.

On the synthetic maps

07 Interactive · the statistician's dilemma

Widen the window, break the physics

The {ν, ν½} basis is collinear: over a narrow scan-rate window the two columns are nearly proportional, so the condition number and variance-inflation factor (VIF) explode and the k₁/k₂ split is undetermined. The obvious fix is to widen the scan-rate range — but a wider range reaches into scan rates where the true exponent b varies widely, so the single-ν½ model is more badly mis-specified. Drag the two handles and watch both sides of the trade move at once.

09 Experiment

Even ferrocene fails

The synthetic study says the method is reliable only in a narrow, capacitance-dominated, reversible corner. Does a real, well-behaved system live there? Ferrocene in TBAPF6/acetonitrile is about as ideal as electrochemistry gets: a fast, chemically reversible one-electron couple on a planar electrode, peak separation 60–80 mV. Recording the blank electrolyte supplies the capacitive current directly, and the subtraction iferrocene − iblank supplies the faradaic current — so the decomposition can be judged against measured ground truth, not an assumed reference.

Against that ground truth the split is unphysical: Dunn's capacitive term overstates the true blank roughly tenfold and has the wrong shape (R² = −597, worse than a constant); the diffusive coefficient takes the wrong sign at 55% of potentials; the assigned capacitive fraction is 40% where the measured value is 4% (ρ ≈ 0.04). The overall fit looks unremarkable (median R² = 0.72, cond = 118, VIF = 14.5) — fit quality is decoupled from partition accuracy.

That this happens for ferrocene is the strongest form of the argument. The failure is not a sluggish couple, a resistive cell, a porous electrode, or overlapping redox — none of those are present. It arises because the fixed {ν, ν½} basis is mis-specified for any real interface: the measured double-layer current scales as να with α ≈ 0.67 (constant-phase behavior), not ν¹, and the faradaic current follows a potential-dependent exponent rather than a clean ν½. If the method manufactures capacitance on ferrocene, the fractions it reports for genuinely disordered pseudocapacitive materials — where no ground truth exists — cannot be regarded as physically meaningful.

10 The way forward

Fit the physics, not the power law

The diagnostics motivate a physics-based inversion. Rather than fitting two collinear power laws point-by-point, the measured voltammograms are described by their governing forward model — the full Butler–Volmer / semi-infinite-diffusion system — and the physical parameters (k°, Cdl, transport constants) are recovered directly by simultaneous inversion across all scan rates and both branches, with identifiability assessed from the parameter covariance. No scan-rate scaling assumption is invoked; the recovered parameters stay physically consistent because the model that generated the data is the model being fit.

Reserved for results: drop in the recovered kinetic parameters, the master-scaling regime map, and the multi-cycle extension as those figures finalize.
